summary: The LRUCache implementation contains a critical correctness bug in its eviction logic: when the cache is full and a new key is inserted, the LRU (least-recently-used) entry is popped from the internal list but is never removed from items_map_, leaving stale entries behind. This causes the map to grow unboundedly over time and can lead to incorrect lookups. Additionally, there is a pervasive performance issue with redundant string copying — std::string is constructed from string_view in multiple hot paths (get/set), causing unnecessary heap allocations that degrade both read and write performance. The shared_lock optimization introduced in LRUCache::get() is valid for improving read concurrency, but it does not address the eviction correctness bug, and the construction overhead persists regardless of the locking strategy. Overall, while there are good intentions toward concurrency, the cache as written is not safe for production use due to the correctness bug and suffers from avoidable allocation costs.

comments.body: When inserting a new key into a full cache, `last = items_list_.back()` is computed and popped from `items_list_`, but `items_map_[last.first]` is never erased. This leaves a stale entry in `items_map_` pointing to a destroyed iterator. Subsequent lookups will use a dangling iterator, and the map grows unboundedly across evictions.

Additionally, the branch order is wrong for the update path: when a key already exists, the code erases from `items_list_` but never removes from `items_map_` before re-inserting. The re-insert `items_map_[std::string(key)] = items_list_.begin();` works, but the value-insert path above must also erase-from-map, otherwise the map accumulates dead entries on every fresh insertion at capacity.

`std::string(key)` is constructed up to 4 times per `set()` (in `find`, push_front key, emplace key). Each copy allocates. Use `items_map_.try_emplace` or store the constructed key once to reduce allocations on the hot write path — relevant since this PR explicitly targets throughput.
comments.suggested_fix: Construct the key once into a local `std::string` and reuse it for lookups and insertions.

comments.body: `get()` uses `std::shared_lock` for the entire call, including the `list_.splice(...)` which mutates the linked list under a shared lock. `std::list::splice` is documented to invalidate iterators of the spliced-from list but does not synchronize against writers; with concurrent `set()` calls mutating the list, this is a data race. Readers can observe a partially-updated list.
comments.suggested_fix: Either use `std::unique_lock` for `get()`, or split the lookup (shared_lock) from the LRU promotion (unique_lock) — promote only if needed and consider skipping promotion under a shared lock to keep the path lock-free for reads.

comments.body: `return it->second->second;` returns a reference into the list node's stored string, but the caller receives `std::optional<std::string>` by value, so a copy is made — fine for safety, but means readers serialize on the underlying allocation anyway. More importantly, if `get()` is changed later to return a `string_view` or reference, the shared lock must be held for the lifetime of the returned view; document this hazard.
comments.suggested_fix: Add a comment noting the returned string is a snapshot and the lock is released after the copy.

comments.body: Data race / logical bug: when capacity is reached, you pop the back node but never erase its entry from items_map_. The map and list become desynchronized — future get() calls may return stale or freed iterators, or miss actual entries. Memory leak also results. Fix: items_map_.erase(last.first); before pop_back.

Even after fix, this whole branch is done under exclusive lock so the second items_map_.find is wasted — reuse 'it' from the lookup above. Also std::string(key) is constructed 3 times per set(): once for find, twice more for the map insert and list node. Each is a heap allocation when key > SSO threshold (~15 chars).

items_map_ uses std::string as both key type and as the lookup argument. Heterogeneous lookup (C++20) would let you pass string_view directly: `items_map_.find(key)` with a transparent comparator (e.g., std::unordered_map with a hasher/view comparator, or std::map with std::less<>). This eliminates the temporary std::string allocation on the hot get() path — relevant since this is the read-heavy path the PR targets.
comments.suggested_fix: Use std::map<std::string_view, ..., std::less<>> or std::unordered_map with transparent hashing so find() accepts string_view without constructing an owning std::string. Store the key as string_view in the list node too.

comments.body: items_list_.splice with a single iterator is O(1) — good. However, the shared_lock is held for the entire splice operation. Under very read-heavy workloads this is fine, but be aware that splice touching the shared list structure means the std::list node pointers are read while another thread may be writing them under the unique_lock in set(). shared_lock vs unique_lock synchronization through std::shared_mutex is correct here (acquire/release on the shared_mutex provides the needed happens-before), so this is safe. No action needed; flagging for clarity only.

Return copies the std::string out of the node — that's a heap allocation for values > SSO threshold on every cache hit. At high QPS this is measurable. Consider returning a string_view into the owned storage (valid until next eviction/overwrite) if callers can tolerate it, or use a small buffer pool.
comments.suggested_fix: If API permits, return std::string_view referencing the node's value; document lifetime. Otherwise consider COW strings or intrusive storage.
